1296.title: Children and rehat
1296.hook: the code says amrit may be taken when one is old enough to understand
1296.howItsDone: Sikh children are named in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and raised with the daily prayers; the Rehat Maryada says amrit should be taken when one is old enough to understand, without setting an age.

segments.voice: Yesterday, coming back after a lapse: a letter of leaving, torn up. Your line was you can return.

A small boy in a gurdwara sits beside his father, a tiny patka on his head, the knot slightly crooked. During the Ardas he stands when everyone stands, a beat late, and folds his hands because his father's hands are folded. He knows some of the words. He doesn't yet know what most of them mean. Is he keeping the rehat? Is he a Sikh yet? The Sikh code has an answer about when the big question gets asked, and it isn't a number on a birthday card.
screen: `A CROOKED KNOT, A LATE STAND.` → `HE KNOWS THE WORDS, NOT YET THE MEANING.` → `WHEN DOES THE QUESTION GET ASKED?`

segments.voice: In the Rehat Maryada's section on amrit, the code says, in paraphrase, that the one being initiated should not be very young, and should have reached an age of understanding. Notice what it doesn't say: there's no number. The measure is understanding. Why? Think of what the initiate is told at amrit: the daily banis, the five articles, the four things never to do. Those are promises, and a promise only means something when the person making it knows what's being promised. Early on, this path called amrit a step, not a pressure. So amrit waits. But waiting isn't leaving the child outside. Earlier in this block you met the naming, where a hukam is taken from the Guru Granth Sahib and the child's name begins with the first letter of that hymn. From the start, the child is brought into the Guru's presence. In families who keep the code, a child's hair is left uncut long before any vow, and the child grows up hearing Japji in the morning and Kirtan Sohila at night, sitting cross-legged in the langar line. That's how a child reaches understanding: not by being told every rule at once, but by living inside the practice first. Some families teach Gurmukhi, the script of the Granth, so the child can read the hymns for themselves. And there's a quiet respect in this. The code doesn't take the choice away by making it too early. It prepares the ground, and waits for the child to step forward on their own.

segments.voice: Think of one rule you keep and how you'd explain it to a child in two sentences, without saying because I said so; if there's no child in your life, explain it to the child you once were. Find the simplest true reason, and say it to yourself once. Then breathe, and notice whether finding it changed how you hold the rule.

1297.title: Rehat at work
1297.hook: keeping the articles of faith in workplaces far from Punjab
1297.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the articles of faith wear them at work, adapting to safety rules and uniforms (a patka or net over the kesh, a kara taped for a shift), and Sikh teaching counts honest earning, kirat, as part of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, children and rehat: amrit waits for understanding, and the child grows up inside the practice. Your line was when they understand.

Five forty-five in the morning, a hospital locker room. A nurse finishes Japji on her phone with one earbud in, ties her hair under a surgical cap, slides her kara up her forearm and tapes it for the shift. Across town a cook pulls a net over his beard before the first ticket prints. On a building site, a foreman raises, once again, the question of a hard hat over his turban. None of them are in Punjab. After the kirpan and the law, something smaller and more daily: an ordinary shift.
screen: `A NURSE, A COOK, A FOREMAN.` → `FAR FROM PUNJAB.` → `AN ORDINARY SHIFT, WITH THE REHAT ALONG.`

segments.voice: Start with the job itself, which in Sikh teaching is part of the path. Early on, you met kirat, honest work, and the line earn it clean. Guru Nanak puts it in one line on Ang 1245, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own effort, and gives some of it away, has recognized the way. Earning isn't a break from the spiritual life; it sits right beside giving. So a Sikh at work isn't stepping out of the rehat for the length of a shift. The workplace is one more place it gets kept. Then the practical side. The articles of faith go to work too. The kesh stays uncut and covered, under a turban, a patka, a cap, a net. The kara stays on the wrist. The kirpan is worn in whatever way the place and its laws allow. That often takes conversations, with a manager, a safety officer, a uniform supplier, and Sikhs in different countries have had them one workplace at a time, with answers that vary. And there's a third side, which belongs to everyone else. A colleague's turban, beard or kara isn't a costume or a quirk. It's a promise, kept on company time. Respect at work can be as simple as asking a real question once, and then letting it be normal.

1298.title: Your rehat
1298.hook: whatever stage you're at, some rule of life can be yours
1298.howItsDone: Some Sikh teachers point to the day Guru Ram Das describes on Ang 305 (rising early, remembering the Name, keeping the Guru's word through the day) as a model of daily practice, for the initiated and for those not yet initiated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat at work: honest earning, and the articles of faith along for the shift. Your line was faith at work.

Some listeners on this path wear a turban and have taken amrit. Some keep their hair and haven't. Some are learning the faith of a partner, a grandparent, a friend at school. Some came because a line of Guru Nanak caught them and wouldn't let go. This block has read a code written with the initiated in mind, so it's fair to wonder where that leaves everyone else. Today the code turns toward you, wherever you are. Not to sign anyone up; just to ask what a way of living looks like when it's small enough to start.
screen: `AMRITDHARI, LEARNING, CURIOUS.` → `A CODE FOR THE INITIATED.` → `WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?`

segments.voice: Guru Ram Das has a passage on Ang 305 that reads less like a rulebook and more like a portrait of a day. In paraphrase: the one who calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and remembers the Name, makes the effort to bathe in the pool of nectar, and keeps the Guru's word on their lips through the day. Sitting or standing, they remember. And that Sikh, the passage says, is pleasing to the Guru. Look at how it's built. Not a list of prohibitions, but a shape: a morning, a day full of remembering, and love at the end of it. The full code sits on top of that shape and fills it in. Early on, your line was a way, not a list. The word rehat means a way of living, how someone carries on day to day, and everyone has one. A person who checks their phone first thing has a rehat. So does a person who skips breakfast and is short with people by noon. The question isn't whether to have one; it's whether to choose it. Nobody here is asked to take a vow. But anyone can borrow the shape of that portrait: something for the morning, something to carry through the day, something to give. Three small rules, chosen on purpose, held for a while, and changed when they stop fitting. Some Sikh teachers describe the faith with three supports of their own: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share.
screen: `ANG 305: A PORTRAIT OF A SIKH'S DAY.` · `A SHAPE, NOT A LIST OF NOS.` · `EVERYONE ALREADY HAS A REHAT.` · then, large: `THREE SMALL RULES, CHOSEN ON PURPOSE.`

1299.title: Rehat and humility
1299.hook: keeping the code does not make one better than others
1299.howItsDone: Sikh teaching sets humility (nimrata) beside the rehat; in the langar, amritdhari and non-amritdhari Sikhs and visitors sit in the same rows and eat the same food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your rehat: a way of living, chosen on purpose, small enough to start. Your line was my three rules.

Any rule kept well comes with a small, quiet danger. Someone starts running at dawn and, a month later, catches themselves glancing at the people still asleep. Someone gives up sugar and starts noticing everyone else's dessert. Keeping a discipline can turn, without anyone meaning it to, into keeping score. A code as full as the Rehat Maryada could make that danger bigger: a Sikh who keeps every line might be tempted to look sideways at a cousin who doesn't. The hymns speak to that danger.
screen: `A DISCIPLINE KEPT WELL.` → `A GLANCE AT THE ONES ASLEEP.` → `KEEPING A RULE, OR KEEPING SCORE?`

segments.voice: Early on this path you met sweetness and humility side by side. Here's how deep it goes. Guru Arjan, in the Sukhmani Sahib on Ang 266, says, in paraphrase: the one who knows themselves to be lowly is counted the highest of all. The ladder is turned upside down; climbing it by your own effort, and announcing it, sends you down. Then Kabir, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own. On Ang 1364, in paraphrase, Kabir says: I am the worst of all; everyone else is good. Whoever understands this, he adds, is a friend of mine. A saint whose words are sung in gurdwaras calls himself the worst. Then a story Sikh tradition tells about the founding of the Khalsa. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, then knelt before those same five and asked them to give amrit to him. A line traditionally sung about that day calls him the Guru and the disciple at once. So the founder of the Khalsa put himself under its vow, and under the very people he'd just initiated. Read beside these three, the code looks like a way to shape a life toward God, not a ranking of who's closer. A Sikh can keep every line and still sit in the langar in the same row as everyone else, eating the same food from the same hands. The rule shapes the one who keeps it. It doesn't make them a judge of anyone who doesn't.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you do well and keep up, a habit, a skill, a prayer, and let yourself be glad about it for a moment. Then bring to mind someone who doesn't do that thing, and notice, without scolding, whether a little score-keeping shows up. Hold that person with the same warmth you just gave your own practice.

1300.title: Rehat and joy
1300.hook: discipline as a frame for a joyful life
1300.howItsDone: Sikhs sing the Anand Sahib in the evening Rehras and as ceremonies close, the wedding is called the Anand Karaj, and the Ardas asks for chardi kala, rising spirits.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat and humility: the Guru kneeling to his own five. Your line was no better than others.

Joy has come, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the opening of the Anand Sahib, a hymn by Guru Amar Das, in paraphrase, and you met it early on this path. Anand means joy, bliss. Sikhs sing it in the evening prayers, its verses are sung as ceremonies close, and the Sikh wedding takes its name from the same word: Anand Karaj, the ceremony of joy. Yet the code is full of disciplines: rise early, cover the hair, refuse the drink, keep the promise. How do the two go together?
screen: `JOY HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.` → `ANAND: JOY, BLISS.` → `A CODE OF DISCIPLINES, A SONG OF JOY.`

segments.voice: Start with how the Guru Granth Sahib itself is built. The heart of it is arranged by raag, a musical measure. Each raag has its own rules: which notes belong, which are left out, the mood it carries, often the time of day it suits. A musician who ignores those rules doesn't get more freedom; they get noise. A musician who keeps them gets music. So the scripture holds its song inside a discipline. Back to the Anand Sahib. Guru Amar Das doesn't say joy came by escaping anything. In paraphrase, it came by finding the Guru, and with it, the hymn says, the raags themselves came to sing the Word. The joy has a source and a shape. Then there's chardi kala, rising spirits, an outlook that keeps lifting. It's in the Ardas, near the end: with the Name, may spirits rise. Sikh tradition holds it up in hard times too; it isn't a mood for easy days only. Set this beside the code. The morning banis frame the day the way a raag frames a song. The kesh, the kara, the clear mind, faithfulness at home, honest work: they're the notes the life is played in. Inside that frame there's room for a lot of joy. A langar hall can be loud with talk and laughter. Hola Mohalla has horses and games. A wedding goes around the Granth to singing. The discipline isn't the opposite of the joy. It's what gives the joy somewhere to live.
screen: `THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAAG.` · `ANAND: JOY WITH A SOURCE.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · then, large: `THE FRAME GIVES JOY A PLACE TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you do on purpose, regularly: a walk, a prayer, a song you practice, a meal you cook the same way. 1301.title: The code close
1301.hook: a shared way of life for a scattered people
1301.howItsDone: Sikhs in different countries follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada as a shared reference, so the daily prayers, the five articles, the ceremonies and the serving of karah prashad look alike from one gurdwara to the next.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat and joy: the raag that frames the song. Your line was discipline and joy.

A small apartment, at evening. A family stands for the Ardas, hands folded, the youngest peeking at the others to see when to bow. Half a world away, a crowded gurdwara does the same, at a different hour of the same turning planet. They've never met. They don't share a climate, a currency, or a first language for their children. But they stand at the same words, bow at the same moment, and hand out karah prashad the same way, into cupped hands. That sameness didn't happen by accident.
screen: `TWO CITIES, ONE EVENING PRAYER.` → `NEVER MET, SAME WORDS.` → `WHAT THE CODE BUILT.`

segments.voice: Flip back through this block like a photo album. It opened with a plain question: who is a Sikh? Then the daily banis, rising early, the sangat and the gurdwara: how the Granth is opened and rested, what may be sung, how the hukam is taken. Readings, karah prashad, katha. No caste, no charms. Daswandh. The turban, a child's naming, the wedding and remarriage, simple funerals. Then amrit: who gives it, what is promised, what happens when it's broken, and the penance that mends it as service. The Guru Panth, the Akal Takht and the jathedars, the Takhts one by one, the Sarbat Khalsa, the older rehatnamas, and why a code was written down at all. Then the body and the day: kesh, turbans, the kirpan and the law, kara and kangha, food, a clear mind, faithfulness at home. And last, the spirit it's kept in: love, return, children, work, your own rehat, humility and joy. What does it add up to? Sikhs live today in countries around the world, and a scattered people could easily have drifted into separate customs. The code gives them a shared shape instead: the same morning prayers, the same articles, the same ceremonies, the same way of serving karah prashad. And a line in the Ardas holds the scattering inside it. In paraphrase: wherever the Khalsa is, there may there be protection and grace. Wherever. The prayer assumes a people spread out, and asks for them all at once. And it isn't the whole story: the panth also holds many orders and schools, each with its own emphasis. That's where the path goes next.

1302.title: Many streams
1302.hook: the panth holds many orders and schools, each with its own emphasis
1302.howItsDone: Sikhs learn from more than one sampardaa: a congregation may hear kirtan in one style, katha from a scholar of another school, and recitation taught by a third, while all bow to the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday the code closed, and your line was one way, many places. Today the one way opens into many streams.

A big city gurdwara on a holiday morning. Near the door stands a man in deep blue, his turban wound high and ringed with steel. Inside, a young student reads from the Granth slowly, every syllable placed like a stone in a wall. In the kitchen, an older man in plain white washes pots. Upstairs, a group has been singing since before dawn. They all bowed to the same Granth on the way in. They didn't all learn their ways in the same place. After weeks with the code that holds the panth together, today we start meeting the streams that run inside it.
screen: `A MAN IN DEEP BLUE AT THE DOOR.` → `A STUDENT READING SLOWLY.` → `A QUIET MAN AT THE POTS.`

segments.voice: The word for a stream like that is sampardaa: a tradition handed on, teacher to student, with its own way of doing things. Over the coming weeks you'll meet several. Some are orders of renunciants who look after shrines. Some are scholars who wrote commentaries. One is known for quiet service, one keeps the old martial life on horseback, one teaches careful recitation, one sings through the night. Each puts its weight on a different thing, and each, in its own telling, traces its line back to the Gurus. In the hymn Sikhs call Sohila, sung at night, Guru Nanak speaks of six schools, six teachers and six teachings. Then, in paraphrase: but the Teacher of teachers is one, appearing in many forms. He was speaking about the schools of his own day, not about Sikh orders that came later. Still, the shape of the thought helps: many ways of teaching, one source. Two honest things belong next to that. First, Sikhs hold a range of views about these streams: how close each stands to the Khalsa's code, where an emphasis becomes a difference. Some of those questions are still argued, and this path won't settle them. Second, a stream is not a wall. A Sikh can learn kirtan from one, pronunciation from another, and service from a third, and come home to the same congregation. So meet each one on its own terms, hear what it cares about most, and rank none of them.
screen: `SAMPARDAA: A TRADITION HANDED ON.` · `EACH LEANS ON SOMETHING DIFFERENT.` · `SOHILA: SIX TEACHERS, ONE TEACHER.` · `A STREAM IS NOT A WALL.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: From the streams you heard about today, the shrine keepers, the scholars, the servers, the riders, the readers, the night singers, choose the one you know least about and hold just its outline in mind, without judging it. Breathe in with the question, what does this one care about most, and breathe out leaving the answer open.
Sampardaa. A tradition handed on from teacher to student, with its own emphasis. The panth holds several, and each traces itself to the Gurus. Today's word.
Your line: many streams, one guru. Each one gets its own day. See you tomorrow.
